PASSO 1: o pretérito imperfecto descreve: STEP 1: the pretérito imperfecto describes the past without saying when it started or when it ended. It's for what used to be habitual, for descriptions, and for the backdrop of a scene. «De niño vivía en Sevilla» (I lived there as a child — no telling how long). STEP 2: for -ar verbs, drop the «-ar» and add: -aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -abais, -aban. «Hablar» becomes «hablaba, hablabas, hablaba, hablábamos, hablabais, hablaban». STEP 3: for -er and -ir verbs, drop the ending and add: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían. «Comer» becomes «comía, comías, comía, comíamos, comíais, comían». «Vivir» becomes «vivía, vivías, vivía, vivíamos, vivíais, vivían». STEP 4: «yo» and «él, ella, usted» share the same form: «hablaba», «comía». When that's ambiguous, add the pronoun: «Yo vivía en Lima y ella vivía en Cusco». STEP 5: the written accent is required on «-ía» (always) and on «-ábamos» (nosotros, -ar). Without it, the pronunciation is wrong — there's no such word as «comia» in Spanish. STEP 6: -ar verbs are spelled with a «b» in «-aba». STEP 7: this tense is regular even for verbs that change their stem in the present: «dormir» becomes «dormía» (not «durmía»), «tener» becomes «tenía», «hacer» becomes «hacía». STEP 8: the typical markers are «de niño», «antes», «siempre», «cada día», «todos los veranos», «a menudo», «normalmente», «entonces», and «mientras».
o português tem o mesmo tempo, o pretéri: English has no dedicated conjugation for this tense at all — it leans on «used to» + infinitive («I used to live there») or just the plain simple past, with context doing all the work of signaling habit versus a one-off event. Spanish, by contrast, marks the distinction directly in the verb's own ending, so «hablaba» can never be mistaken for a single finished action the way English «I talked» can mean either a habit or a one-time event depending on what surrounds it. Because English gives you no verb-shape cue to lean on here, the endings themselves — and especially the written accent on «-ía» and «-ábamos» — are the part worth drilling hardest.
As a child I used to work at a bank.
When I was little, we used to live near the sea.
My grandparents used to have a vegetable garden.
The written accent on «-ía» is required.

Ser, ir, ver e quando usar o imperfecto: Ser, ir, ver, and when to use the imperfecto
PASSO 1: só três verbos são irregulares: STEP 1: only three verbs are irregular in the imperfecto: «ser», «ir», and «ver». STEP 2: «ser» becomes era, eras, era, éramos, erais, eran. «Ir» becomes iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, ibais, iban. «Ver» becomes veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veíais, veían. STEP 3: the accent shows up in «éramos» and «íbamos»; in «veía» it marks the strong «i». STEP 4: the first use is a past habit: «Todos los veranos íbamos al pueblo» (every summer we'd go to the village). Sentences like this talk about what used to repeat. STEP 5: the second use is describing people and things in the past: «Mi abuela era alta y llevaba gafas» (my grandmother was tall and wore glasses). STEP 6: the third use is age, time, and weather: «Tenía diez años», «Eran las ocho», «Hacía frío», «Llovía». STEP 7: the fourth use is setting the scene or a state: «La casa estaba en una colina», «Mi tío estaba cansado». STEP 8: in all these cases the fact has no clear beginning or end. For a single, closed-off fact (ayer, el lunes), go back to the indefinido. Lesson 22 covers that choice. STEP 9: in Latin America, «de chico, de chica» is common in place of «de niño, de niña», and «de grande» in place of «de mayor».
em português: «eu era, eu ia, eu via» co: English «was/were» and «used to go» map closely onto «era» and «iba» for description and habit, so that part feels familiar. What's new is that Spanish treats age, time, and weather in the past (tenía diez años, eran las ocho, hacía frío) as part of this same imperfecto system — a single grammatical category — where English just uses its ordinary past tense for all of these with no special marking at all («I was ten», «it was eight o'clock», «it was cold»), so there's no verb-shape cue in English to flag this as a distinct use.

PASSO 1: «mientras» liga duas ações que: STEP 1: «mientras» connects two actions that were happening at the same time; the verb goes in the imperfecto on both sides: «Mientras yo cocinaba, mi padre leía» (while I was cooking, my father was reading). STEP 2: «exquisito» doesn't mean «exquisite» in the narrow English sense of finely crafted — it just means delicious, really good, or refined: «La comida era exquisita». To say something's odd or strange, use «raro» or «extraño»: «Es un hombre muy raro». STEP 3: «embarazada» doesn't mean «embarrassed» — it means pregnant: «Mi hermana estaba embarazada». To say «embarrassed», use «avergonzado» or «cortado»: «Estaba muy avergonzada». STEP 4: «antiguo» means old in the sense of historic or long-standing; «viejo» means old in the sense of worn or aged. «Una casa antigua» isn't necessarily run-down. STEP 5: the imperfecto also shows up with time and age, as in the previous section: «Eran las cinco y ya era de noche» (it was five and already dark).
três pares enganam o brasileiro: «exquis: Two of these false friends are genuine traps for an English speaker, just from a different direction than for a Portuguese one: «exquisito» looks like English «exquisite» and does share some of its meaning (refined, very good), but it's used far more broadly in Spanish for anything delicious, which can feel like overkill applied to, say, a sandwich. «Embarazada» looks nothing like English «embarrassed» on the page, so an English speaker is less likely to fall into that one by resemblance — but it's worth knowing precisely because the two words can otherwise seem like they should be related. «Raro» maps cleanly onto English «rare» in spelling but means «odd/strange» far more often than «uncommon» in everyday Spanish.
